What sets arthropods apart from other invertebrates?
They have soft bodies with no skeleton
The manual says what sets arthropods apart from other invertebrates is that they have segmented legs.
Which of these animals is NOT an arthropod?
Worms, jellyfish and leeches lack backbones but do not have segmented legs, so they are not arthropods.
What type of external skeleton do arthropods have?
A soft, leathery skin with no skeleton
A shell made of calcium only
Arthropods have a chitinous (hard) external skeleton.
Which arthropod is given as an example of a body with only a head and body?
Ticks have a head and body; spiders have a cephalothorax and abdomen; butterflies have a separate head, thorax and abdomen.
In spiders, what is the fused head and thorax called?
Spiders have the head and thorax fused into a cephalothorax, plus an abdomen.
How many pairs of legs does an insect have?
Insects have three pairs of legs, one pair of antennae and a body in three parts.
Into which three parts is an insect's body divided?
Insect bodies are divided into three distinct parts: the head, thorax and abdomen.
Which insects are examples of the ametabolic (no metamorphosis) life cycle?
The ametabolic life cycle (egg - young - adult) is the most primitive; examples are fish moths, springtails and bristletails.
What are the stages of the hemimetabolic (incomplete metamorphosis) life cycle?
Hemimetabolic (incomplete metamorphosis) is egg - nymph - adult, e.g. dragonflies, aphids, bugs and termites.
In the hemimetabolic life cycle, what is each moult of the nymph called?
Nymphs moult their exoskeleton as they grow, and each moult is called an instar.
In the holometabolic life cycle, during which stage does the body structure change completely?
During the pupa stage the body structure changes completely before the adult emerges.
Which group of insects has a holometabolic (complete metamorphosis) life cycle?
Ants, bees, wasps, butterflies and beetles
Holometabolic (egg - larva - pupa - adult) examples are ants, bees, wasps, butterflies and beetles.
Which insect larvae feed on horns and hooves, which most other animals cannot digest?
The larvae of the horn-borer moths feed on horns and hooves, helping with nutrient and mineral recycling.
According to the manual, how do the diseases passed on by insects affect the ecosystem?
They help regulate populations of plants and animals
They have no effect on populations
They increase the amount of pollination
Insects pass on a variety of diseases that help to regulate populations of both flora and fauna.
How do termites help to 'unlock' nutrients from dead plants?
Symbiotic organisms help them break down cellulose
They burn dead plant material in their mounds
They store the plant material without digesting it
They feed the plant material to dung beetles
Through symbiotic relationships with protozoa, fungus and others, termites break down cellulose in dead plants so nutrients can be recycled.
Which termite caste is made up of infertile males and females with undeveloped sexual organs?
Workers and soldiers are infertile males and females whose sexual organs have failed to develop, so they can devote time to labour.
Workers that tend the fungus gardens
Young nymphs that have not moulted
Alates are winged fertile males and females, present in the mound in spring and summer; they are feeble fliers.
How do termite workers stimulate the queen to lay more eggs?
They fan her with their wings
The workers lick the queen to stimulate laying; when she is old they eventually lick her to death.
Under optimal conditions, queen termites may live for over...
The manual states that, under optimal conditions, queen termites may survive for over 45 years.
The 'cement' that binds fungus-growing termite mounds is made of...
Large fungus-growing termite mounds are soil particles bound with 'cement' of termite excrement and saliva.
How can you tell where harvester termites are living?
Small, scattered heaps of loose sand with a hole in the centre
Tall mounds that lean towards the north
Harvester termites live in underground chambers; small heaps of loose sand with a central hole show where they are.
What is true of the harvester termite queen?
She can move around the nest, as there is no royal chamber
She lives in a royal chamber at the top of a mound
She lives alone, outside the main nest
She is licked to death within her first year
In harvester termite nests the queen can move from one part of the nest to another and there is no royal chamber.
What are a mantid's two front legs armed with for grasping prey?
Mantids stalk and grasp prey with their two front legs, which are armed with a double row of spikes.
How does the female mantid make her egg case?
She secretes a liquid that turns into foam in the air
She spins a silk cocoon from her spinnerets
She chews wood pulp and spit into a nest
She rolls a ball of mud around the eggs
The female secretes a liquid from her genital opening that turns into foam on contact with the air, then lays about 60 eggs in it at night.
How does a cicada produce its shrill sound?
A muscle repeatedly clicks a membrane on the side of its body
It scrapes its legs along its abdomen
It forces air out through its mouth
A muscle attached to a membrane on either side of the body contracts and releases, making clicks repeated in quick succession.
What do cicada nymphs feed on while living underground?
The nymph falls to the ground, buries itself and feeds on the roots of the tree, for a couple of years up to seventeen years.
How do antlion antennae differ from those of dragonflies?
Antlion antennae are clubbed and conspicuous
Antlion antennae are threadlike and minute
The antennae of the antlion are clubbed and conspicuous, whereas those of the dragonfly are threadlike and minute.
What is unusual about antlion larvae?
They have no anus and store their waste until the end of the larval stage
They have no mouthparts and do not feed
They can glow in the dark
Antlion larvae lack an anus; all their waste is stored and ejected as a single pellet at the end of the larval stage.
How long can the antlion larval period last?
The larval period can last up to three years, after which the larva spins a silk cocoon and pupates for about four weeks.
What kind of insects are glow-worms and fireflies?
Glow-worms and fireflies are neither flies nor worms; they are beetles.
Which enzyme in firefly blood acts on luciferin to produce light?
An enzyme called luciferase acts upon luciferin in the presence of oxygen to produce light; urate crystals act as a reflector.
How does a firefly switch its light on and off?
By controlling the flow of oxygen to the light cells
By opening and closing its wings
By controlling the flow of oxygen to the cells, the insect can switch the light on and off at will.
Which group of dung beetles rolls a brood-ball away from the dung heap before burying it?
Telecoprids roll a brood-ball away from the dung, lay an egg in it and bury it.
Which group of dung beetles steals dung balls from other dung beetles?
Kleptocoprids steal dung balls from the telecoprids.
Which group of dung beetles lays its eggs directly into the dung?
Endocoprids lay their eggs directly into the dung; paracoprids bury a dung ball directly below the dung pile.
Without dung beetles, how much of the nitrates in a dung heap would seep into the soil?
Without dung beetles only 3% of the nitrates would seep into the soil; the rest would be left on the surface.
Why were dung beetles introduced into Australia?
As a biological control for flies breeding in cattle dung
To feed birds on cattle farms
Australia had no natural way to recycle cattle dung; introduced dung beetles greatly reduced the dung left for flies to breed in.
Which insect group is described as by far the most medically important of all insects?
Flies, midges and mosquitoes pass on many diseases such as malaria, sleeping sickness, nagana and anthrax.
Why can male mosquitoes not suck blood?
They have no proboscis at all
The male's mouthparts are imperfectly developed and cannot pierce skin; he feeds on nectar and fruit juices.
What does it mean when a female mosquito is 'autogenous'?
She can lay her first batch of eggs without a blood meal
She never needs blood to lay eggs
She can lay eggs without mating
She feeds only on nectar all her life
An autogenous female can lay her first batch of eggs without a blood meal, but later egg-laying requires blood.
What causes the very high fever in malaria?
Toxic by-products released when infected red blood cells burst
Mosquito saliva left in the bite wound
Toxic by-products from the protozoa feeding on red blood cells are released when the cells burst, causing high fever and delirium.
What is the usual incubation period of malaria after a bite?
The incubation time for malaria is usually between 10 and 14 days, but can be shorter or much longer.
When do most malaria infections happen?
Malaria increases in years of heavy rainfall, with most infections happening in late summer.
How does a resting tsetse fly hold its wings?
Folded one over the other like the blades of scissors
Spread out flat to the sides
Tsetse wings are folded one over the other like the blades of a pair of scissors, with the tips beyond the abdomen.
Which tsetse flies feed on blood?
Both sexes of tsetse fly are blood-feeders (sanguinophagous).
What does sleeping sickness cause in the body?
Swelling of the brain and inflammation of the heart
Bursting of red blood cells only
Tsetse flies carry the protozoa; the infection spreads through the blood and causes swelling of the brain and inflammation of the heart.
How do butterfly antennae usually differ from moth antennae?
Butterfly antennae are usually clubbed at the end
Butterfly antennae are threadlike and minute
Butterfly antennae are usually clubbed; moth antennae are usually feathery and never clubbed at the tip.
A device that links the wings together in flight
A scent pouch on the hind wing
A scale that sheds when touched
A frenulum links the wings together in flight; most moths have one and butterflies do not.
What is the main food plant of the mopane moth larva?
The main food plant of the mopane moth larva is the leaf of the mopane tree.
Why are African monarch butterflies toxic to predators?
Their larvae eat poisonous milkweed leaves
They produce venom in their scent glands
They feed on poisonous nectar as adults
The larvae eat the poisonous leaves of milkweed, making both caterpillar and adult butterfly toxic.
Why is the female African diadem seldom preyed upon?
She closely mimics the toxic African monarch
She has large eye-spots on her wings
The female African diadem is not toxic but closely mimics the African monarch, so she is seldom preyed upon.
What prompts the mass migration of brown-veined white butterflies?
Numbers grow far beyond the food available
By December the population grows far beyond food availability, prompting mass migration in a north-easterly direction.
Which ants are the soldiers of the colony?
Workers are sterile females of different sizes; the major workers have large heads and are the soldiers.
What happens when an attacked ant releases a large amount of alarm pheromone?
The rest of the colony flees
Other ants come in to help
The colony moves into the attack
Limited secretion calls in support from the colony, while large amounts make the rest of the colony flee.
What does a female spider-hunting wasp do with the spider she has stung?
Lays her egg in it so her larva can feed on it alive
Uses it to build her nest
Feeds it to the adult wasps in the colony
She carries the paralysed spider to her nest and lays an egg in its abdomen; the larva feeds on the living spider.
How does a female fig-wasp find a fig of the right species?
Each fig species releases its own chemical pheromone
She follows other wasps to the tree
She recognises the colour of the fruit
She is attracted by the sound of the tree
Each fig species releases a specific chemical pheromone which the wasp picks up with her well-developed antennae.
What type of relationship exists between figs and fig-wasps?
Figs depend totally on fig-wasps for fertilisation and the wasps depend on figs; this is obligate mutualism.
What do paper wasps build their nests from?
Paper wasps are communal insects that build their 'paper nests' from wood-pulp and spit.
Which statement about honey bee drones is correct?
They come from unfertilised eggs and cannot sting
They are sterile females that forage
They are the only bees that can sting
Drones are males from unfertilised eggs; they cannot sting and their only purpose is to mate with a virgin queen.
What happens to honey bee drones at the onset of winter?
They are kept out of the hive and die
They mate with the old queen
They hibernate in the centre of the hive
When the nectar flow falls in winter, drones are no longer allowed into the hive and die of exposure and/or starvation.
What is the final duty of a worker honey bee?
After about three weeks of nursing, guarding and fanning, the worker's final duty is foraging.
Which bee product is described as the optimal natural antibiotic?
Propolis is the optimal natural antibiotic and acts against fungi, bacteria and viruses.
How should a bee sting be removed?
Scrape it out with a knife blade in the direction it went in
Squeeze it out between finger and thumb
Pull it out with tweezers by the venom sack
Leave it in until it falls out
Scrape the sting out with a knife blade in the same direction it went in, without squeezing more venom from the sack.
Which of these can trigger bees to become aggressive?
Sweat, engine fumes and the smell of crushed khaki weed near a hive can trigger bees.
According to the manual, what is the best defence if bees attack?
The best defence is to run through thick bush, or close yourself in a tent or building if possible.
How many body parts do arachnids have?
All arachnids have two body parts: the cephalothorax and an abdomen.
What does it mean that an arachnid's body is a haemocoel?
Blood circulates without the aid of tubes
The body is filled with air sacs
The blood is pumped through veins
The arachnid body is a haemocoel - it circulates the blood without the aid of tubes.
According to the manual's comparison table, what do spiders eat?
The table states that insects are herbivores and carnivores, while spiders are carnivores.
From what did spider venom glands originate?
Spider venom glands originated as accessory digestive glands, and the venom aids external digestion.
Where are a spider's sense organs for smell and touch found?
On the legs, as slits or fine hairs
A spider's sense organs for smell and touch are on the legs as slits or fine tactile hairs that pick up vibrations.
What is the female spider's reproductive organ called?
The male places sperm with his pedipalps into the female's reproductive organ, the epigynum.
What is the process of moulting in arthropods called?
The process of moulting in arthropods is called ecdysis; young spiders moult up to 10 times.
At which trophic level are spiders classified?
Spiders are secondary consumers because their prey are usually primary consumers.
What are the two primary functions of spider venom?
To kill or paralyse prey and start breaking down its organs
To defend the web and attract mates
To build egg sacs and paralyse prey
To scare predators and mark territory
Spider venom kills or paralyses prey and then starts breaking down the internal organs before the prey is eaten.
What is the first step of first aid for a serious neurotoxic spider bite?
Wash the site of the bite
Raise the limb above the heart
Wash the bite, apply a crepe bandage, then a cold compress, keep the limb below the heart and get to a medical facility.
After a neurotoxic bite on an arm or leg, where should the limb be kept?
Below the level of the heart
Above the level of the heart
If the bite is on an extremity, keep the limb below the level of the heart to restrict the flow of venom.
In the neurotoxic venom group, which spider requires immediate action?
The manual says that in the neurotoxic venom group only the black widow requires immediate action.
What is typical of a cytotoxic spider bite at first?
It is usually painless and symptoms are slow to appear
It causes immediate severe pain and paralysis
It causes breathing difficulty within minutes
It causes heavy bleeding from the bite
A cytotoxic bite is usually painless with slow symptoms: a red, swollen, itchy area like a mosquito bite.
In first aid for violin and sac spider bites, how should the wound be iced?
For 10-minute intervals at least twice a day
Ice the wound for 10-minute intervals at least twice a day and apply antiseptic cream.
Where does the name 'baboon spider' come from?
Their colour and hairy, stout body
They are often eaten by baboons
They live in baboon sleeping sites
The noise they make in a threat display
The colour and hairy, stout body are the origin of the name baboon spider.
How are the different horned baboon spider species best identified?
By the location of the horn on the cephalothorax
By the colour of their fangs
By the depth of their burrows
By the pattern on the abdomen
Horned baboon spiders are best identified by the location of the horn on the cephalothorax; their venom is neurotoxic.
How does the six-eyed crab spider catch its prey?
It buries itself just below the sand and ambushes prey
It spins a large orb web
It chases prey over long distances
It hunts in groups from a communal nest
The six-eyed crab spider ambushes prey, buried just below the surface where sand sticks to its body.
How many eyes does the violin spider have?
The violin spider has six eyes, whereas most other spiders have eight.
What does a sac spider bite look like at first?
Two red dots about 6 mm apart
A large blister with a black ring
The sac spider bite shows two red dots about 6 mm apart; effects are only noticed about 24 hours later.
How can the brown widow be told apart from the black widow?
An orange/red hour-glass shape under the abdomen
A red dot on the upper side of the abdomen
A preference for long grass and rocks
The brown widow has an orange/red hour-glass under the abdomen; the black widow has a red dot or stripe on top.
How does the brown widow's egg sac differ from the black widow's?
It has small spikes sticking out
It is flat against a surface
It is buried in the sand
Both have whitish, ball-shaped egg sacs; the brown widow's has small spikes, the black widow's is smooth and round.
Where are community web spiders commonly seen?
In large, messy nests on thorn trees in the savannah
In burrows up to 30 cm deep
These social spiders build large, messy ball-shaped nests in a community on thorn trees in the savannah.
What is the stinger at the end of a scorpion's tail called?
The tail ends in a stinger called an aculeus; the segment before it contains the venom gland.
What do scorpions use their enlarged pedipalps (pincers) for?
The chelicerae are used for feeding and the pedipalps (pincers) are enlarged for capturing prey.
Where do young scorpions stay until their first moult?
The young climb onto the female's back and remain there until their first moult, then scatter.
How long can some larger scorpions live?
Smaller species may live 3-5 years, but some larger scorpions can live for as long as 25 years.
Scorpions dig 'keyhole' shaped burrows; in hot dry areas they are deep to keep the scorpion cool.
Why should campers be careful when sitting around a fire?
Logs thrown on the fire often disturb scorpions
Logs thrown onto a camp fire often disturb scorpions, so campers should take care.
Which scorpion family has thick tails and thin pincers?
Buthidae have thick tails and thin pedipalps; Scorpionidae have thin tails and thick pincers.
How venomous are scorpions of the family Scorpionidae?
The most venomous in southern Africa
Scorpionidae have thin tails and thick pedipalps used to hold prey, and are only mildly venomous.
How do thick-tailed scorpions make a loud hissing sound?
By scraping the sting along the first tail segments
By forcing air out of their book-lungs
By beating their legs on the ground
They rasp the sting along the first two or three tail segments (stridulating) to warn predators.
How do burrowing scorpions mainly subdue their prey?
Burrowing scorpions do not rely on their sting to kill prey but rather on their powerful pincers.
How does the manual describe the sting of the bark scorpions?
Extremely painful but not medically significant
The smaller bark scorpions have an extremely painful sting but are not medically significant.
What feature separates the granulated thick-tailed scorpion from other thick-tailed scorpions?
Its aculeus is about half the size of the other tail segments
It has thin tails and thick pincers
The aculeus is about half the size of the other tail segments; colour alone can be confusing.
Which scorpion is described as the most venomous species in southern Africa?
The granulated thick-tailed scorpion is the most venomous species in southern Africa.
Which scorpion is known to spray venom when agitated?
The Kalahari thick-tailed scorpion is known to spray venom when agitated.
What type of venom do scorpions of the family Buthidae have?
Mild venom with no effect on the heart
Buthidae venom is neurotoxic with powerful cardiotoxins that affect the heart muscle; it can also paralyse breathing.
What is the correct order of first aid for a scorpion sting?
Wash, crepe bandage, cold compress, immobilise below heart
Cold compress, wash, raise limb above heart
Cut the wound, suck out venom, then bandage
Give aspirin, wash, then apply a tourniquet
Keep the patient calm, wash the sting, apply a crepe bandage, then a cold compress, and immobilise the limb below heart level.
Which pain relief must NOT be given for a scorpion sting?
Aspirin should not be taken to alleviate the pain, nor should pethidine or morphine be given.
Why is it important to identify which scorpion stung the patient?
A more specific anti-venom exists for the granulated thick-tailed scorpion
So that the patient can be given aspirin
Because only bark scorpions need treatment
So the scorpion can be released safely
A more specific anti-venom was made for the granulated thick-tailed scorpion, so good identification is important.
Why are solifuges not true spiders?
They lack silk-producing organs and venom glands
Solifuges are not true spiders as they lack silk-producing spinning organs and venom glands.
Which part of a solifuge is often mistaken for a fifth pair of legs?
Solifuge pedipalps are long and are often mistaken for a fifth pair of legs.
How do female solifuges care for their young?
She guards the eggs and stays until the young have moulted once
She carries the young on her back until they mature
She leaves the eggs buried with no care
She feeds the young on a dung ball
The female lays about 20 eggs in late summer, guards them and stays with the young until they have moulted once.
Which is the largest mite and the only one easily seen?
The velvet mite is bright red, about 5 mm, and is usually seen after summer thundershowers.
What is the short projection that carries a tick's mouthparts called?
Tick mouthparts are on a short projection called a gnathosoma.
Ticks form an important food source for which birds?
Ticks are consumers in the trophic pyramid and an important food source for oxpeckers.
A bacterial infection in the tick's saliva
A virus spread by tick droppings
Tick-bite fever (rickettsia) is caused by a bacterial infection transmitted in the tick's saliva.
What is the incubation period of tick-bite fever?
The incubation period from bite to symptoms is 5 - 7 days; it can be treated with antibiotics such as doxycycline.
Without treatment, about how many people infected with Congo fever will die?
Without treatment, around 30% of people infected with Congo fever will die, usually within two weeks.
What is the incubation period of Q disease?
Q disease has an incubation period of two to three weeks; the fever lasts about 7 to 14 days.
What feature do hard ticks have that soft ticks do not?
Hard ticks have a dorsal shield or scutum and mouthparts visible from above.
How many legs do newly hatched hard tick larvae ('pepper ticks') have?
The eggs hatch into minute 6-legged larvae, often called seed ticks or pepper ticks; nymphs have 8 legs.
Where are the mouthparts of soft ticks (tampans) found?
On the underside, not visible from above
On the first pair of legs
Soft tick mouthparts are on the ventral side (underside) and are not visible from above.
How many pairs of legs does each centipede body segment have?
Each centipede segment has one pair of legs (excluding the first and last two segments).
Does a centipede bite need medical attention according to the manual?
No - it is painful but does not need medical attention
Yes - it is always fatal without anti-venom
Yes - it causes severe tissue necrosis
Although centipede venom is painful, it does not require medical attention.
The male leaves sperm on the ground for the female to take up
The male places sperm with his pedipalps
The male spins a web for his sperm
The female lays eggs that the male fertilises in water
The male deposits sperm on the ground for the female to engulf; this is indirect internal fertilisation.
How many pairs of legs do most millipede body segments have?
Each millipede segment has two pairs of legs, except the first four segments (the thorax), which have one pair each.
Which animals are named as major predators of millipedes?
The manual states that civets are major predators of millipedes.
How do millipedes protect themselves from predators?
They wriggle like a snake and release a foul chemical
They spray venom from their tail
They hide inside a silk web
Millipedes have a hard exoskeleton, wriggle like a snake and release a foul chemical to prevent attack.
